Ohio Economy Dashboard

Conditions and a one-year statistical outlook for Ohio, its large metros, and the U.S.

Data through Sep 2026 · Updated Sep 27, 2026

At a glance

Snapshot for Aug 2026: a mid-cycle expansion with a still-tight labor market. Currently: labor still tight; activity on the firm side; inflation near normal; ordinary house-price growth. That reading is backed by low unemployment, low UI claims, firm activity growth. Over the next year the central paths lean toward a bit more cooling in activity, with labor still relatively steady. No clear recession-style warning in the major labor and activity paths. For additional regional intelligence covering all of Ohio (and the rest of the Fourth District), the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland is a valuable source—especially its SORCE survey and Fourth District Beige Book.

One-glance read aligned with the summary above. Green = favorable, yellow = caution, red = concerning.

Ohio Downturn Probability (turning-point signal)

As of Sep 2026, the model puts the probability that Ohio's economy is in a coincident-index decline at 0% (low); the probability of a decline 3 months ahead is 0% and 6 months ahead 8%. The long-run share of decline months since 2000 is 12%. The coincident index itself is published through Aug 2026.

Probit models of an Ohio downturn month, defined as a fall in the Philadelphia Fed Ohio coincident index over the previous three months (shaded), on the 3-month average of the model's national and Ohio factors (national1, national2, ohio1, ohio2); one direct probit per horizon (now, 3 and 6 months ahead). COVID months are excluded from estimation and blanked in the chart. In-sample fit uses smoothed factors and overstates real-time accuracy; treat this as a research signal, not an official recession call. See Methods §5b.

Ohio Industry Composition (GDP shares)

As of 2025, Ohio’s largest GDP contributors include Finance, insurance & real estate, Manufacturing, Professional & business services. Manufacturing alone is about 14% of Ohio GDP versus roughly 9% nationally—Ohio remains a goods-heavy state. Finance/real estate and health care are large service anchors alongside professional services and government. Shares are current-dollar BEA GDP by industry (structural snapshot, not a monthly cycle gauge).

Annual GDP by industry, current dollars (BEA Regional table SAGDP2N). Bars show each sector’s share of statewide (or U.S.) GDP for the latest available year (2025). Top sectors by Ohio share; U.S. shares shown for comparison. Source: BEA GDP by State.

Ohio Goods Trade Trends

In 2025, Ohio shipped about $57 billion in goods exports. Exports were about -2% versus 2024. Goods imports were about $87 billion the same year (merchandise trade deficit of roughly $31 billion). Manufactured goods account for the bulk of shipments (about 94% of exports). On the latest detailed partner snapshot (2022), the largest markets include Canada (34%), Mexico (13%), Japan (6%), China (5%). Trade data are merchandise only (not services), concentrated in vehicles, machinery, and other industrial products.

Annual totals of monthly Census goods trade for Ohio (FRED EXPTOTOH / IMPTOTOH), calendar years with full 12 months. Partner shares use Census/Origin-of-Movement annual series via FRED (latest detailed year). Source: FRED / U.S. Census Bureau.

Fourth District Business Survey (Cleveland Fed SORCE)

As of the Aug 2026 survey wave, Cleveland Fed SORCE diffusion indexes summarize whether more Fourth District contacts report increases than decreases in current conditions, employment, and expected conditions (positive = net expansion among respondents). These are soft, timely regional survey readings—not official Ohio hard data—and complement the hard series above. Coverage is the Federal Reserve’s Fourth District (all of Ohio plus parts of PA, KY, and WV).

Seasonally adjusted diffusion indexes from the Cleveland Fed Survey of Regional Conditions and Expectations (SORCE) for the Total sector. Index = percent reporting increases minus percent reporting decreases (range −100 to +100; zero ≈ balance). Released about eight times per year. Source: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland — SORCE (doi:10.26509/frbc-sorce). Not estimated inside the DFM; shown for regional context.

Methodology & model details

This dashboard reports forecasts from a hierarchical mixed-frequency dynamic factor model (MF-DFM) estimated on Ohio, Midwest, and national series from FRED. The state unit is monthly. Quarterly series are observed only in quarter-end months (March, June, September, December); other months are missing for those series. Charts show rate levels or year-over-year percent growth only (never QoQ/MoM).

Cleveland MSA geography: OMB redefined the metro (Bulletin 23-01): the area is now titled Cleveland, OH (not Cleveland-Elyria); Elyria was dropped as a co-named principal city and the county footprint was revised (including Ashtabula). This dashboard and the residual factor cleveland1 use only BLS/FRED series labeled Cleveland, OH (MSA) (area codes 17410 / 391741). All legacy Cleveland-Elyria series (CLEV439*, CBSA 17460, LAUS/CES 391746, ATNHPIUS17460Q) are excluded from the estimation panel and charts.

1. Observation equation (estimation space)

Let \(i\) index series and \(t\) months. After transform and standardization, the observation equation is

\[ z_{i,t} = \alpha_i + \Lambda_i' F_t + \varepsilon_{i,t} \]

where \(z_{i,t}\) is the demeaned/scaled estimation-space series, \(F_t\) is the vector of latent factors active for series \(i\) (see loading table), \(\Lambda_i\) are free loadings on those factors (zeros elsewhere), and \(\varepsilon_{i,t}\) is idiosyncratic noise. Fourier seasonal terms (annual and semi-annual harmonics) are residualized from the panel before factor extraction so latent factors are non-seasonal; the same terms re-enter the observation regression and series forecasts. Optional COVID dummies may also enter in sample; forecasts set COVID dummies to zero.

Transforms into estimation space:

  • Growth / index series: \(g_t = 100\,\log(Y_t / Y_{t-1})\) (monthly) or QoQ log growth at quarter ends.
  • Rate series (unemployment, yields, fed funds): \(\Delta r_t = r_t - r_{t-1}\) (first difference; avoids mean-reversion of levels to the long historical average).

Each transformed series is standardized using means and standard deviations computed from 2000-01-01 onward (hard COVID window excluded from location/scale).

2. Factor hierarchy and extraction

Factors are extracted stagewise by residualized EM-PCA, then loadings are estimated by OLS with the hierarchy mask:

  1. National factors \(F_t^{\mathrm{N}}\) from the national panel only. Residualize all series on \(F^{\mathrm{N}}\).
  2. Ohio residual factors \(F_t^{\mathrm{OH}}\) from non-national residuals. Residualize non-national series on \(F^{\mathrm{OH}}\).
  3. MSA residual factors \(F_t^{m}\) for each metro \(m\) in {cleveland, columbus, cincinnati} from that metro’s residual panel. Residualize those series on \(F^{m}\).
  4. Sector block factors \(F_t^{b}\) for \(b\) in {labor, prices, housing, activity} from residualized series in each block.
  • National factors: 2
  • Ohio residual factors: 2
  • MSA residual factors: 1 each for cleveland, columbus, cincinnati
  • Block factors: 1 per block (labor, prices, housing, activity)
  • Total factors: 11 — national1, national2, ohio1, ohio2, cleveland1, columbus1, cincinnati1, labor1, prices1, housing1, activity1

Estimated factor paths (history and short-horizon forecasts) for each layer of the hierarchy are plotted on a companion page: factor paths (research view).

3. Which series load on which factors

✓ = free loading estimated; blank / — = restricted to zero. “Own block” means labor / prices / housing / activity matching the series catalog.

Series groupNational

ohio*		MSA residualSector block
labor* etc.
National (US GDP, CPI, UNRATE, FEDFUNDS, …)✓———
Ohio state / regional (OHUR, OHRQGSP, Midwest CPI, …)✓✓—own block
Cleveland MSA series✓✓own only

Compactly, for a series with allowed factor set \(S_i\):

\[ z_{i,t} = \alpha_i + \sum_{k \in S_i} \lambda_{i,k} f_{k,t} + \varepsilon_{i,t} \]

\(S_i\) = national factors only for national series; national + Ohio residual + own block for state/regional series; national + Ohio + own MSA residual + own block for MSA series.

4. Factor dynamics (sparse VARX)

Factors follow a sparse hierarchical VARX (not independent ARs):

\[ F_t = c + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \Phi_j F_{t-j} + \Gamma X_{t-1} + u_t \]
  • Lag order: \(p = 2\) (selected by sparse-VARX BIC over candidates [1, 2, 3, 4, 6]; common sample, hierarchical lag restrictions; picks by criterion on this run: BIC p=2, AIC p=6, HQIC p=3; re-selected on every build, not fixed; a real-time backtest of p is pending)
  • Sparsity: national factors depend only on national lags; Ohio on national+Ohio; each MSA on national+Ohio+own MSA; blocks on national+Ohio+own block.
  • Exogenous \(X\) (national financial/activity and cycle indicators, lag 1, in Ohio/MSA/block equations): FEDFUNDS, GS10, INDPRO, PAYEMS, UNRATE, CFNAI, BBKMLEIX, NFCI, T10Y3MM, SAHMREALTIME, WEI (AR(1) for multi-step \(X\) paths). CFNAI, the Brave–Butters–Kelley leading index, NFCI, the 10y–3m term spread (T10Y3MM), the real-time Sahm rule and the NY Fed Weekly Economic Index enter in levels (they are stationary indexes); NFCI and WEI are weekly and enter as monthly means of complete weeks. Missing values at the ragged edge are carried forward; before a driver's first observation (WEI starts 2008) its sample mean is used.
  • Kalman smoother: factors refined by a joint linear Gaussian filter/smoother given hierarchical loadings and the VARX law (Mariano–Murasawa poly for quarterly series).
  • Extraction weights: majors up-weighted in EM-PCA (×3).

5. Idiosyncratic residual, direct multi-horizon, and forecasts

Let \(\hat\varepsilon_{i,T}\) be the last in-sample residual in estimation space. Forecasts add a decaying AR(1) residual path so short-horizon forecasts do not jump from the last data point to the pure common component:

\[ \hat\varepsilon_{i,T+h} = \rho_i^{h} \hat\varepsilon_{i,T}, \qquad \hat z_{i,T+h} = \alpha_i + \Lambda_i' \hat F_{T+h} + \hat\varepsilon_{i,T+h} \]

Direct multi-horizon: for major indicators, also estimate \(z_{i,T+h} = a_{i,h} + b_{i,h}' F_T\) by OLS for \(h \in \{1,2,3,4,5,6,9,12\}\) and blend with the iterated VARX common-component path.

Factors are iterated with the sparse VARX (Monte Carlo draws of shocks for bands). Mapping back to levels:

  • Growth series: compound from last level, \(Y_{T+h} = Y_T \cdot \exp\!\big(\sum \hat g / 100\big)\); quarterly growth is applied as \(g/3\) per month for a monthly latent path (MM used in Kalman measurement).
  • Rate series: \(r_{T+h} = r_T + \sum \widehat{\Delta r}\).

Dashboard display for indexes is year-over-year growth of the level path, \(100\,\log(Y_t / Y_{t-12})\). Confidence bands: 350 Monte Carlo simulations; 68% (16th–84th) and faint outer 95% (2.5th–97.5th) percentiles. Chart history ≈ 3 years, January-aligned; forecast horizon 12 months.

5b. Turning-point (downturn) probabilities

An Ohio downturn month is defined as \(D_t = 1\) when the Philadelphia Fed Ohio coincident index (OHPHCI) is below its level three months earlier. For each horizon \(h \in \{0, 3, 6\}\) a direct probit \(\Pr(D_{t+h}=1 \mid F_t) = \Phi(a_h + b_h' \bar F_t)\) is estimated, where \(\bar F_t\) is the 3-month average of the national and Ohio factors (national1, national2, ohio1, ohio2). Because the factors are Kalman-smoothed to the edge of the panel, \(h=0\) is a nowcast even for months the coincident index has not yet covered. COVID months (covid_start to covid_soft_end) are excluded; an L1-regularized probit is used if separation occurs. In-sample probabilities use two-sided factors and overstate real-time accuracy; a pseudo-real-time (ALFRED vintage) evaluation is in progress. Probabilities are written to turning_point_probabilities.csv.

Latest run (factors through Sep 2026; coincident index through Aug 2026): h=0: 0%, h=3: 0%, h=6: 8%. McFadden pseudo-R²: h=0: 0.79, h=3: 0.48, h=6: 0.25. Share of downturn months since 2000: 12%.

6. Sample & robustness

  • Weekly data: Ohio initial claims, continued claims and the insured unemployment rate (OHINSUREDUR) are weekly; each enters as the monthly mean of complete weeks (weeks assigned by week-ending date). The current month is missing until its last week is published, so a partial month never looks like a collapse in claims, and continued claims (a stock) are never summed.
  • Freshness: each build polls FRED metadata for every series in the panel and re-downloads any series with a newer observation or a newer revision date; alternative sources (EIA, Zillow, BLS, BEA) are refreshed when their cache is older than 7 days.
  • Removed in v1.1: Ohio leading index OHSLIND (discontinued 2020), KYOHURN (Ohio County, KY), invalid catalog IDs, and the Ohio JOLTS series (BLS now publishes state JOLTS once a year). Midwest CPI components and BLS average prices are assigned to the prices block. Columbus and Cincinnati unemployment rates use the seasonally adjusted LAUS series (COLU139UR, CINC139UR).
  • Estimation sample: 2000-01-31 to 2026-09-30 (144 series after filters)
  • Factor sample start: 2000-01-01
  • COVID handling: dummies (2020-03-01–2020-12-31; soft tail to 2021-06-30)
  • Growth / Δr winsorization: 0.5% tails
  • Advanced flags: VARX=True, Kalman=True, MM=True, direct=True
  • MSA dashboard packs: Columbus (18140) and Cincinnati (17140): unemployment, employment, manufacturing, FHFA HPI. Cleveland (current 17410): unemployment, employment, manufacturing, Case-Shiller Cleveland HPI, labor force. Building permits are not plotted on the dashboard.

7. Data sources

Primary and alternative series used in estimation and on this page (programmatic downloads; free public APIs / open CSVs):

  • FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis) — fred.stlouisfed.org · API docs: docs (Ohio/MSA/national labor, housing, GDP, CPI, rates, weekly UI claims and insured unemployment rate, etc.; also the national cycle drivers: Chicago Fed CFNAI, Brave–Butters–Kelley indexes, NFCI; NY Fed Weekly Economic Index; real-time Sahm rule; 10y–3m Treasury spread)
  • BLS Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) — bls.gov/jlt · Public API: developers (U.S. job openings rate. Ohio state JOLTS are no longer used: since 2026 BLS publishes state JOLTS once a year, so they are not a timely monthly input.)
  • EIA electricity retail sales — eia.gov/opendata (Ohio total and industrial sales, MWh)
  • BEA Regional Economic Accounts — bea.gov regional · API: API signup (Ohio real GDP and personal income; metro regional price parities)
  • Zillow Research public data — zillow.com/research/data (ZORI rents and ZHVI home values for Cleveland, Columbus, Cincinnati metros; attribution to Zillow Research required)
  • Census / BLS via FRED — high-propensity business applications and other formation series where available (e.g. BAHBATOTALSAOH on FRED)
  • BEA GDP by State (industry) — bea.gov (annual current-dollar GDP by industry for Ohio industry-composition panel)
  • U.S. Census goods trade (via FRED) — EXPTOTOH / IMPTOTOH monthly goods exports and imports for Ohio (annualized on the trade-trends panel; partner shares from Census SCEN series)
  • Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland — SORCE (Survey of Regional Conditions and Expectations) — SORCE page · doi:10.26509/frbc-sorce (Fourth District diffusion indexes; all of Ohio plus parts of PA, KY, WV; plotted on this dashboard for context, not inside the DFM)

Cleveland charts use the current Cleveland, OH metro definition (BLS area 17410). Geography details are in the Cleveland note above.
